stem: James Doherty, a 66-year-old man, presents complaining of nervousness.
Background. He is a known case of atrial fibrillation. He was taking flecainide; his cardiologist changed him to amiodarone four weeks ago. He has come today for his blood test results.
Results handed to you in the room: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal, 0.4–4.0) · Free T4 28 pmol/L (high, 10–20) · Free T3 8.9 pmol/L (high, 3.5–6.5).
tasks: Take a focused history
Interpret the investigation results for the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Roughly 4–4:30 history, 1:30 results, 2:00 diagnosis and differentials.

back.dx: Thyrotoxicosis with INAPPROPRIATE TSH secretion — high T4/T3 with a NORMAL TSH. Two diagnoses, in order: (1) TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma; (2) amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction (honest caveat: amiodarone should suppress TSH, and four weeks is early — but TSH can drift back to normal over months, so it stays on the list). The station is built on one mismatch: in thyrotoxicosis the TSH should be suppressed and his is not. Say it to the examiner, and a lay version to the patient. Hidden agenda: wants the amiodarone stopped today; underneath, frightened his heart is getting worse.
plan: Confirm ID; 'I have your results and we'll go through them — first, what do you mean by nervous: stressed and on edge, shaking hands, or racing heart?'
Timing, pattern, impact (4 weeks, since the switch — note it, don't close on it)
AF anchor: how long, adherence, WHY was flecainide changed, side effects, follow-up; complications — racing, chest pain, SOBOE, oedema, TIA/stroke symptoms, anticoagulant
Track 1 thyroid: heat intolerance, bowels, weight loss, sweating, tremor. Track 2 pituitary: headache, blurred vision, side vision, weakness/numbness
Psychiatry + stimulants: mood, sleep, 'I ask everyone — thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?', home/stress, tea/coffee, alcohol, substances, cold-and-flu tablets

Results in FOUR rungs: gland in the neck makes hormones → yours are high → TSH from the brain controls it → when hormones rise TSH should fall; yours stayed normal — that mismatch is what I must explain. 'Does that make sense so far?'
'Two things on my list' — adenoma (usually not cancer), then amiodarone with the honest caveat. Three ready answers: cancer? stop the tablet? what now? Then the rest of the differentials

Plan: repeat assay on a different platform (ask about biotin), further hormones incl. cortisol, formal visual fields, pituitary MRI, endocrinology; speak to cardiologist yourself; red flags; phone with the repeat result
ask: Can you tell me what you mean by feeling nervous? Stressed and on edge, shaking in your hands, or a racing heart?
How long? Constant or comes and goes? Getting worse? Anything make it better or worse? How is it affecting your day-to-day life?
Why was the flecainide changed? Are you taking the amiodarone regularly, exactly as prescribed?
Still getting racing? Chest pain? Breathless on exertion, ankle swelling? Any weakness/numbness one side, trouble speaking, brief loss of vision? On a blood thinner?
Heat intolerance? Looser/more frequent bowels? Weight loss? Sweating? Shaking hands?
Headaches? Blurred vision, or difficulty seeing to the sides? Weakness or numbness anywhere?
How has your mood been? Your sleep? 'I ask everybody this — any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?'
Who do you live with, any stresses at home or work?
How much tea/coffee? Alcohol? Other substances, cold-and-flu tablets? Any supplements — biotin?
pefe: No examination in this station — results are handed to you

Investigations to name: repeat TFTs on a different assay platform (artefact/biotin), full pituitary hormone profile including MORNING CORTISOL, formal visual field testing, pituitary MRI; endocrinology referral; discuss with cardiologist
To the examiner: 'This is thyrotoxicosis with inappropriate TSH secretion' · 'My first investigation is a repeat assay on a different platform'

Examiner challenge — start carbimazole today? NO: mechanism unknown; if TSH-oma a thionamide lowers T4 and drives TSH higher; if type 2 amiodarone thyroiditis the gland isn't overproducing — thionamide won't help. Repeat assay, involve endocrinology first
fails: Assuming what 'nervous' means and launching a thyroid history without asking
Agreeing 'it's just the tablet' — false reassurance that abandons the normal TSH
Skipping 'why was the flecainide changed?'
Asking mood and sleep but NOT self-harm — marked down hardest
Not asking headache and vision (the pituitary track)
Giving one diagnosis instead of two, in order
Telling him to stop the amiodarone, or not offering to contact the cardiologist
Physiology lecture: drawing the axis, saying 'negative feedback'; jargon without 'in plain English'
numbers: TSH 1.8 normal · fT4 28 · fT3 8.9 both high · 4 weeks on amiodarone — early for drug-induced thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis requires a LOW TSH — except in pituitary disease
Amiodarone thyroid phases: hyper → hypo → normal, over months
Five causes of normal TSH + high T4: assay artefact (biotin), sampling/timing, amiodarone late phase, TSH-secreting adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance
Before any thyroid-directed treatment in pituitary disease: check cortisol first
Five history blocks — block 5 is psychiatry

Variant 1 (early recall): TSH 0.02, 8 months on amiodarone = overt amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis; separate type 1 vs 2 with colour-flow Doppler; endocrine + cardiology together before changing the drug
Variant 2: headaches + clipping door frames = bitemporal field defect → urgent fields, MRI, neurosurgery, cortisol first
Variant 3: high-dose biotin, no symptoms = artefact; stop, wait days, repeat on different platform — VERIFY washout interval
'Is it cancer?' — usually benign, treatable, not what I'm worried about today · 'Stop the tablet?' — no, it holds your rhythm; I'll speak to your cardiologist myself
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450

stem: You are a GP. Jenny Alderton, 37, has come in with palpitations and dizziness for three days.
(Version A — shorter stem.)
tasks: Take a focused history (4–5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. 4–5 minutes history, ~30 seconds ECG, remainder diagnosis with a named cause. Ask for vitals before you begin.

back.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response — vitals BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98%: stable but tachycardic. Duration THREE DAYS, CONTINUOUS (>48 h — dictates the whole rhythm-control answer). Hidden clue only if asked about associated symptoms: months of exertional chest tightness and breathlessness up the hill, settling on rest → the named cause is probable ischaemic heart disease, with coffee, alcohol and smoking contributing. Father MI in his fifties. Hidden agenda: 'Is this what my dad had?' and can't afford time off work.
plan: 'Before I begin, could I please have the vital signs?' → name 'tachycardic, irregular, haemodynamically stable' out loud
WIPE, open question, empathy line. Choose PALPITATIONS as the structure — dizziness in one clarifying question (spinning vs faint; actually fainted?)
Characterise: tap it out; sudden/gradual; constant or comes and goes (3 days continuous); triggers; associated chest pain, SOB, sweating, presyncope

Cause sweep, fast: heart (exertional pain — how long?, orthopnoea, PND, oedema, murmur/BP), lungs (cough, fever, pleuritic pain, calf, travel, snoring), thyroid (weight, heat, tremor, bowels, neck lump), habits (coffee, alcohol, smoking, drugs), PMH/meds/allergies/FHx

ECG — all seven steps, no pauses: rate (10-second bypass line), rhythm irregularly irregular, no P waves/fibrillatory baseline, PR not measurable, QRS just over 2 small squares, up-sloping ST V2–V3 not pathological, T waves unremarkable → 'AF with rapid ventricular response'

Name it, explain it plainly, then the CAUSE (arteries — chest tightness uphill; caffeine/alcohol/smoking). Differentials delivered as causes: thyroid, hypertension, valve, peri/myocarditis, PE, hormone tumours; also anxiety, hypoglycaemia, anaemia
Safety-net (chest pain, severe SOB, syncope, one-sided weakness/droop → 000), summary, invite questions, answer 'is this what my dad had?'
ask: Can you tap out on the desk what the beat feels like?
Did it come on suddenly or build up? Constant for the three days, or comes and goes? ★
Does anything set it off — coffee, alcohol, exercise, stress?
With the palpitations — chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, feel like you might black out? ★ (this is where the exertional chest tightness comes out)
The dizziness — spinning, or like you're about to faint? Have you actually fainted?
Breathless lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling? Ever told you have a murmur, high BP, heart problem?
Cough, fever, sharp pain on breathing, calf swelling, long travel? Snore or sleepy in the day?
Weight loss, feeling hot when others don't, tremor, loose bowels, neck lump?
Coffee, alcohol, smoking, other drugs? Other conditions, medications, allergies, heart problems in the family?
pefe: Vitals from the examiner first: BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98% RA
ECG seven steps in order: rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → T; impression AF with RVR

stem: Alan Prosser, 58, presents to the Emergency Department with central chest pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward, with a flu-like illness a week ago.
Vitals: T 37.2 · HR 88 · BP 128/76 · RR 18 · SpO2 97%.
ECG handed to you: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No PR depression, no widespread concave elevation.
tasks: Take a history (4–6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG
Explain the diagnosis and immediate management
time: 8 minutes. The history sounds like pericarditis; the ECG overrides it.

back.dx: Acute INFERIOR STEMI — territorial ST elevation (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal change (I, aVL) = infarct, whatever the story. Pericarditis history + infarct ECG: treat the infarct. Name the mismatch to the examiner: this is exactly why ECG and troponin are part of the pericarditis work-up. Obtain V4R for right ventricular involvement → if RV involved, NO nitrates, give fluid (preload dependent).

ECG aloud: 'Rate 88, sinus, normal axis. ST elevation in II, III, aVF — the inferior leads — with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No widespread elevation, no PR depression. Territorial pattern with reciprocal change = acute inferior STEMI, not pericarditis. I would obtain right-sided leads.'
To the examiner: acknowledge the history suggested pericarditis; the ECG overrides it; treating as infarct
To the patient: tracing shows something more serious — an artery supplying your heart is blocked, a heart attack; the pain didn't feel typical but the tracing is clear; acting now, calling cardiology

Immediate management: resus area, monitoring, O2 only if hypoxic, IV access, aspirin 300 mg chewed, second antiplatelet + anticoagulation per protocol, analgesia; reperfusion — primary PCI if prompt, otherwise thrombolysis + urgent transfer; V4R → avoid nitrates/give fluid if RV; watch for arrhythmia and heart block

'Probably a muscle strain' or 'just anxiety' — fail

stem: You are the doctor in the emergency department. James Okafor, 22, has presented with sudden onset chest pain that started while he was exercising today. He is already on oxygen when you enter the cubicle.
Information available: HR 98 · BP 122/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% · T 36.8 °C · alert and orientated.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Version A: at about five minutes a chest X-ray is provided — explain the X-ray to the patient. Version B: ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

back.dx: Primary spontaneous LEFT pneumothorax, no tension — tall slim 22-year-old, daily vaper (since 18, occasional cannabis), rowing machine, no knock. Pain: left, can point to one spot, sudden, sharp stab, 4/10, constant, no radiation, MUCH WORSE ON DEEP BREATH, leaning forward and rest/activity make no difference. PEFE (Version B): trachea midline · reduced expansion L · hyper-resonant L · absent breath sounds L · reduced vocal resonance L · JVP normal, apex undisplaced, no murmur · no calf asymmetry · ECG pending. Hidden agenda: 'Is it my heart? People my age drop dead' — and a Bali trip in three weeks with a learn-to-dive course. The station in one line: say 'pleuritic' out loud, run the whole structure anyway, name the trachea, protect the last two minutes.
plan: Four vitals (BP, pulse, RR, temp) or the online closed statement; WIPE; open question; empathy ONCE, properly
SOCRATES in full — 'is it an area, or can you point to one spot?' — then the THREE named modifiers: deep breath? rest vs activity? leaning forward?
Say the conclusion aloud: 'sharp, well-localised, sudden, worse on breathing in — we call that pleuritic; it points me towards your lungs rather than your heart. I still need to check both.'

CVS block in FULL: SOB/sweating/nausea; BP/DM/lipids/smoking/FHx; cocaine/amphetamines; fever/flu, leaning forward; orthopnoea/PND/oedema/congenital; ever fainted, esp. on exercise; FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH (ask here, not at the end)

Respiratory: calves, travel, immobility, family clots, haemoptysis; WHAT EXERCISE and any knock/tackle; previous pneumothorax self/family; smoke/vape/cannabis; fever/cough/phlegm; 'unlikely at your age but I ask everyone' weight loss/lumps/night sweats
GI (heartburn, waterbrash, food), MSK (rash, pressing, twisting), psych (stress, mood); SADMA, PMH, allergies, concerns

BELL — X-ray script, six steps, 60–75 s, trachea named even though normal; answer 'am I going to be alright?' with two reasons (trachea central, BP normal) then finish. Version B: PEFE by named items, interpret the card aloud

Diagnosis 30–40 s plain → three reasons (sharp, pleuritic, X-ray/PEFE) → HCM, PE, infection each with a reason → the rest as a rapid list → drain, admit, repeat X-ray, stop vaping, no flying until healed, no diving ever without surgery, safety-net
ask: Where exactly — an area, or can you point to one spot? When, what were you doing, sudden or gradual? Sharp/dull/heavy/tight/burning? Go anywhere? Out of ten? Constant or waves, worse?
Anything better or worse? Specifically — does a deep breath make it worse? Change with rest or activity? Does leaning forward help? ★

SOB, sweating, nausea? BP/diabetes/cholesterol? Smoke? Family heart disease? Cocaine or amphetamines? Fever/chills/flu-like illness? Breathless walking/lying flat, wake at night, ankle swelling, born with a heart condition? Ever fainted, especially during exercise?
Any family history of sudden cardiac death — anyone who died suddenly and young, during sport or in their sleep? ★
Calf swelling/pain? Long flights/car trips, surgery, immobility? Clotting problems in the family? Coughed up blood?
What exercise were you actually doing — and did you take any knock or tackle to the chest? ★
Ever had a collapsed lung, or anyone in the family? Smoke, vape, cannabis? Fever, cough, coloured phlegm? Weight loss, lumps, night sweats?
Tummy pain, vomiting, heartburn, sour fluid? Related to food? Rash on the chest, worse on pressing or twisting? Stress at home or uni, mood? Medications, allergies, past history, operations?
What are you worried it might be?

The finding is ABSENT MARKINGS beyond a visible pleural edge, not blackness — trace apex to costophrenic angle for the subtle apical one

Poor paper film: 'The print quality makes fine detail difficult — clinically your symptoms and examination point to a left pneumothorax, and that's what I can see at the edge; I'd review the digital image'

Version B PEFE by name: general appearance/distress/cyanosis/drowsy; vitals on air and on O2; expansion symmetrical? TRACHEA midline or deviated? bruising/focal tenderness? percussion resonant/hyper-resonant/dull? breath sounds present and equal, added sounds, rub? vocal resonance? JVP, apex, S1/S2, murmurs; abdomen; oedema and calf asymmetry; ECG?

Interpret aloud: reduced expansion + hyper-resonance + absent breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance on the left, trachea midline, BP normal = left pneumothorax without tension; hyper-resonance = air (dull would be fluid/consolidation/haemothorax)
fails: Shortcutting to lung questions once 'pleuritic' is reached — the structure is the mark
Never acknowledging the fear, or sympathising after every answer and reaching 5:00 with half a history
Asking only the open 'better or worse?' and accepting 'nothing really'
Leaving sudden cardiac death to the end and running out of time
Not asking what exercise / any knock (separates spontaneous from traumatic)
Skipping malignancy or psychogenic questions because he's 22
Not commenting on the trachea (Version B: not asking 'midline or deviated?' — the pass-or-fail question) ★
Radiology language to a frightened 22-year-old
Accepting 'air entry reduced on the left' as the whole examination — expansion, trachea, percussion, vocal resonance are four separate marks
The beautiful 40-second physiology explanation that eats the differential time; never finishing the list ★
Tension variant: 'I'd get an urgent chest X-ray to confirm' — the sentence that fails the station ★

Tension = hypotension + trachea deviated AWAY + distended neck veins → clinical diagnosis, no imaging: needle decompression 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line (2nd ICS MCL traditional alternative), then intercostal catheter — decompression is temporising
Drain: safe triangle, 5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line, small-bore 8–14 Fr; symptomatic or unstable → intervene; otherwise conservative/ambulatory with review
Recurrence ~30%, mostly within 1–2 years; vaping/smoking cessation is the single best prevention
Flying: not until resolved, typically a week beyond; diving: never without definitive surgery

Variant 2 HCM: central tightness on running, eased on stopping, near-syncope, uncle died in sleep at 38, NOT pleuritic → ECG + echo; autosomal dominant, commonest cause of SCD in young athletes; ESM louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting (opposite of AS); ECG LVH, deep narrow Q, TWI; cardiology, no competitive sport, avoid dehydration/nitrates/diuretics, screen first-degree relatives

Safety-net: more breathless, worse pain, faint, racing heart, blue lips/fingers → 000

stem: Your next patient is a 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset chest tightness and shortness of breath that began while watching a movie at home. He has had similar episodes before and was told nothing was wrong. His parents are separated, he lives alone, works as an accountant, and has been under stress.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 96 · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 99% RA · alert, anxious.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the pathophysiology of the condition
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · diagnosis 1:00 · differentials 1:15 · pathophysiology 1:15 · management and close 0:30.

back.dx: Panic attack → PANIC DISORDER with agoraphobic avoidance (Daniel Pike, 25). Peak within 5–10 minutes, settled over half an hour; pounding heart, sweating, dizziness, trembling, PERIORAL AND FINGER TINGLING (hyperventilation fingerprint), derealisation. Five or six attacks over three months, mostly out of the blue (desk, train, supermarket queue); two prior ED visits with normal tests. Three key questions make the diagnosis: fear of dying? worried about another? changed behaviour? (stopped cinema, drives instead of train). Also: 5–6 coffees + energy drinks; 'I'm generally an anxious person' (bait for GAD — screen by criteria, don't relabel). The trap: the psychosocial stem is bait — run a CHEST PAIN history and reach the psychogenic bucket LAST. Hidden agenda: convinced doctors keep missing a heart problem; privately frightened he's going mad.
plan: Vitals → open question → acknowledge the 'nothing wrong' frustration explicitly → signpost: tightness, then breathing, then rule out important causes
Full pain analysis INCLUDING 'how long did it take to reach its worst?' and how it settled
Breathlessness in three questions
CVS + RS sweep (note the tingling — use it later); GI, MSK/rash; caffeine/energy drinks QUANTIFIED, drugs, alcohol, recently stopped anything; thyroid symptoms
ANNOUNCE the negative organic screen out loud, then ask permission to move to the episodes
Characterise: how many, over what period, out of the blue or triggered, what was happening in the film, trembling/choking/unreal
THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS verbatim → agoraphobia screen → GAD by criteria → stressors → mood → self-harm

Diagnosis: attack, then disorder; 'your symptoms are real'; 'not in your head — in your body' → differentials of CHEST PAIN with why each is less likely (still do ECG, TFTs) → pathophysiology (alarm system, adrenaline, over-breathing/CO2, vicious cycle; peaks ~10 min, not dangerous) → CBT, MHTP, SSRI low and slow if needed, no benzos, cut caffeine, limit tests, safety-net
ask: Where exactly? When and how quickly? How long did it take to reach its worst? ★ Tight/sharp/heavy/burning? Travel? Out of ten? Better or worse — breathing, moving, position, pressing? How long, how did it settle?
What do you mean by shortness of breath? Better/worse? Cough, noisy breathing, wheeze?

Sweating, nausea, racing, dizziness with it? Smoke, BP, DM, lipids, family heart disease? Fever/flu, better leaning forward? Flat/pillows/leg swelling, ever fainted esp. exercise? Long travel/sitting still, calf swelling/pain, haemoptysis? Chest injury? Fevers, chills, phlegm, weight loss, lumps?
Abdominal pain, vomiting, acid/heartburn, related to eating? Worse on moving or pressing? Rash?
How much coffee or energy drink a day? ★ Recreational drugs, alcohol? Recently stopped anything? Weight loss, feeling hot, tremor, loose bowels?
'I've asked about your heart, lungs, stomach and chest wall and haven't found anything pointing that way — now I'd like to ask about the episodes themselves. Is that all right?' ★
How many, over what period? Out of the blue or a trigger? What was happening in the film? Trembling, choking, things not quite real?
During the attack, did you feel you were going to die — were you afraid of dying? ★
Since then, have you been worried about having another attack? ★
Have you changed any routines or behaviour because of that worry? ★

Places you avoid — public transport, crowds, queues, shopping centres, far from home alone? Apart from the attacks, excessive hard-to-control worry about everyday things — how long? Restless, tired, irritable, tense, poor sleep? What's been happening at home and work? Mood? Thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn't worth living?
pefe: No examination task. Investigations: ECG · FBC, electrolytes/renal, TFTs, glucose · drug screen if indicated — then STOP; 'I don't want to keep repeating tests, because that feeds the worry'

Differentials of the COMPLAINT, each with why it's less likely: ACS/angina (25, no risk factors, non-exertional, no radiation — still ECG) · PE (no travel, no calf, no haemoptysis, sats normal) · pneumothorax (no injury, normal exam/sats) · pericarditis (no viral illness, no positional change) · arrhythmia (possible — ECG) · reflux/ulcer (no heartburn, no meal relation) · chest wall (pressing doesn't reproduce) · thyrotoxicosis and caffeine (bloods) · GAD possible alongside — the attacks define it

Technical pathophysiology if asked: amygdala/sympathetic activation → catecholamine surge (tachycardia, ↑CO, sweating, tremor); hyperventilation → hypocapnia, respiratory alkalosis → cerebral vasoconstriction (light-headedness, derealisation), ↓ionised Ca (perioral/peripheral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm); catastrophic misinterpretation → positive feedback; conditioned anticipatory anxiety and avoidance → panic disorder → agoraphobia
fails: Taking a psychiatric history instead of a chest pain history because you recognised the recall ★
Not acknowledging the 'nothing wrong' frustration
Skipping time-to-peak
Hearing the tingling and moving on
Omitting caffeine/stimulants and thyroid rows
Not announcing the negative organic screen before switching
Saying 'probably anxiety' without the three key questions ★
Relabelling as GAD on 'I'm an anxious person'
'It's just anxiety' / 'there's nothing wrong' / 'try to relax' — marked communication failures ★
Differentials given as a list of anxiety disorders
Prescribing benzodiazepines; repeating investigations
numbers: Panic attack: abrupt surge peaking within minutes (typically <10), ≥4 of 13 symptoms, characteristically fear of dying/losing control
Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month of worry about further attacks OR maladaptive behaviour change
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 of public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues/crowds, outside home alone; typically 6 months
GAD: excessive hard-to-control worry about multiple matters ≥6 months with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, tension, sleep disturbance — discrete attacks not a core feature
Organic mimics: arrhythmia · thyrotoxicosis · hypoglycaemia · asthma · stimulant use or withdrawal

Management: validate → CBT first line → Mental Health Treatment Plan → SSRI if needed, start low go slow, warn of early worsening → avoid benzodiazepines (dependence, safety behaviour reinforcing avoidance) → cut caffeine/alcohol/stimulants → follow-up
'Will I have to take tablets forever?' — CBT is first line; medication only if needed and reviewed
Variant 1 lifelong worrier: panic disorder primary, possible comorbid GAD — name and treat the attacks first, same approach helps both
Variant 2 snake scene, lifelong fear: specific phobia — triggered attack, similar therapy
Variant 3 organic swap: pleuritic pain, 16-hour drive, right calf ache, SpO2 93% → Wells, CTPA, treat as PE until proven otherwise

setting: You are the doctor working in the Emergency Department.
stem: Jack Mitchell, 40 years old, has presented complaining of chest pain for the last two days. He is a known case of schizophrenia.
Vital signs available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient
Explain your initial management to the patient

back.dx: Stable angina (ischaemic heart disease) in a man whose cardiometabolic risk is driven by risperidone — central heaviness to the neck, 6/10, brought on by walking and stairs, settles in a few minutes with rest, NEVER at rest, longest episode five minutes. Vitals normal (BP 138/86, PR 82, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98%). Risk load: father MI at 50, pack a day since 20, 6–8 beers most nights, takeaway diet, no exercise, 20 kg gain on risperidone, nobody has checked lipids or sugar in years. Discriminating question: 'do you ever get this pain when you are resting?' — that answer is the diagnosis. Version B: a voice at night and 'people are giving me this pain' — validate, gently decline the belief, carry on. Hidden agenda: frightened of dying like his father; frightened of being dismissed as 'in my head again'.
plan: Vitals from the examiner BEFORE greeting; intro, name, confidentiality statement (unless risk of harm to you or someone else)
'Tell me more about this pain' — silence; empathy line
SOCRATES as one fluent run; then the discriminator out loud: pain at rest? longest episode?
Signpost, then four schizophrenia questions: when diagnosed, treatment, taking it regularly, side effects (weight, postural dizziness, tremor, dry mouth), GP/psychiatrist follow-up
Three-question screen in order: harm to self or others → hear/see/feel things others don't → anyone trying to harm or control you. Version B: one sentence of validation, note it, move on
CVS risk factors as one continuous run: family MI/stroke, BP/cholesterol/diabetes, smoking, alcohol, drugs, diet, exercise
System sweep in one breath: ACS features, pericarditis, heart failure, PE, chest injury/cough, weight loss/lumps, GORD, MSK/rash; other conditions, meds, allergies
Diagnosis: name it, plain-words mechanism, THREE reasons (pain character, risk factors, the antipsychotic); five-second differential insurance line

Management in three headings: find it (ECG + troponin now, stress test ± echo) · protect the heart (aspirin, statin, GTN, Quitline, alcohol, diet, walking) · fix the cause (do NOT stop risperidone; speak to psychiatrist re switch e.g. aripiprazole, mental health review) · 000 safety-net · summary, questions
ask: Before I begin, could I have Jack's vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?
Everything we talk about stays between you and me — unless there's a risk of harm to you or to someone else. Is that alright?
Jack, tell me more about this pain. → 'I'm sorry to hear that, and I completely understand your concern. I'll do my best to find the cause today.'
Point to exactly where? Sharp, burning, or a heaviness? Out of ten? Travel anywhere? Comes and goes or constant? Brings it on? Makes it better?
★ This next question is important: do you ever get this pain when you are resting — sitting still, or lying in bed at night? And what's the longest one has lasted?

I saw you have schizophrenia — can I ask a few quick questions? It may actually be relevant to your chest pain. When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Able to take it regularly? Side effects — weight gain, dizzy on standing, shaky hands, dry mouth? See your GP and psychiatrist regularly?

★ I ask everyone this: any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else? Do you ever hear, see or feel things other people don't? Do you ever feel anyone is trying to harm you, or controlling you?
Version B reply: 'That sounds frightening, and I can hear how distressing it is. I don't see it the same way you do — but I have no doubt the pain is real, and I'm taking it seriously.'

Anyone in the family had a heart attack or stroke? Ever told high BP, cholesterol or diabetes? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol — how much a week? Recreational drugs? What do you usually eat in a day? Any regular exercise?

With the pain: sweating, SOB, nausea, racing heart? Fever or recent flu-like illness, worse lying flat / better sitting forward? Breathless lying down at night, leg swelling? Long travel, calf pain or swelling? Chest injury, cough, phlegm? Weight loss, appetite, lumps? Tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste, related to eating? Rash, worse on pressing or moving? Other conditions, medications, allergies?

Diagnosis to patient: 'ischaemic heart disease — stable angina. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart has narrowed, not blocked. When you walk the heart needs more oxygen than the narrowed tube can deliver — that shortage is the heaviness. When you rest it settles.' No atherosclerosis / ischaemia / stenosis

Three reasons: character of the pain (central, heavy, to the neck, exertional, relieved by rest) · risk factors (father at 50, smoking, weight, diet) · the medication he takes for schizophrenia raises heart risk
Differential insurance line (5 s): 'no sign you're having a heart attack, though we'll check; I also thought about inflammation around the heart, a clot on the lung and reflux — they don't fit'

Safety-net: pain at rest, >10 min, or with sweating/vomiting/breathlessness → 000, don't drive. Summary + invite questions
If the examiner challenges investigations: ECG + serial hs-troponin to exclude ACS because symptoms are new; functional testing (stress ECG/echo) establishes stable angina; CTCA per local pathway
fails: Never asking about pain at rest and episode duration ★
Omitting the harm-to-self / harm-to-others question ★
Saying the pain is stress, anxiety or part of his illness ('it's in my head again')
Stopping or promising to stop the risperidone; changing it yourself rather than via the psychiatrist
Chasing a full MSE after the delusion and abandoning the chest pain; colluding with or arguing against the belief
Skipping vitals; skipping diet and exercise; giving the diagnosis with no reasons; MONA / aspirin-plus-troponin as the whole plan; no stress test named

Stress ECG positive: ST depression ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping; Bruce protocol increments every 3 min VERIFY

Aspirin 100 mg daily (300 mg stat if ACS) · atorvastatin 40–80 mg nocte · metoprolol 25–50 mg BD · GTN 400 microg SL q5 min up to 3, 000 if pain persists 10 min after first dose · 150 min moderate activity/week VERIFY

Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring: baseline, 3 months, then at least annually · premature FHx: first-degree male <55, female <65 (father 50) · life-expectancy gap in severe mental illness 15–20 years, mostly cardiovascular

setting: You are the doctor on duty at a rural hospital.
stem: Bernard Hollis, 68, has attended with two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness following an episode of gastroenteritis last week. He has chronic kidney disease stage 4 and takes ramipril, spironolactone, metformin and atorvastatin. His blood results have just returned and are on the desk.
K⁺ 7.2 · Na⁺ 134 · urea 24.1 · creatinine 312 · eGFR 16 · HCO₃ 16 · corrected Ca 2.18. BP 104/62 · PR 52.

State the likely causes
Outline your immediate management
Explain the situation to the patient
time: 8 minutes. The ECG is only handed over if you ask for it.

back.dx: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes — AKI on CKD 4 (prerenal from gastroenteritis), ACE inhibitor + spironolactone, metabolic acidosis; hidden ibuprofen for his knee (only if you ask about NSAIDs). plan: Reading time
Write five things: ECG + monitor now, ask haemolysis · PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE · doses · stop ramipril/spironolactone/NSAIDs/trimethoprim · four causes
First sentence
'The potassium is 7.2 — severe. I'd attach cardiac monitoring and get a 12-lead ECG immediately, and check whether the sample was haemolysed'
ECG

Rate · P · PR · QRS · T, in that order → 'changes of severe hyperkalaemia, needs treatment now'. If asked 'ischaemic T waves?' — hyperacute T waves are broad-based and asymmetrical; the flat P, long PR and wide QRS make hyperkalaemia the explanation
Biochemistry
Creatinine 312 / eGFR 16 = advanced renal impairment; urea 24 with prerenal pattern = AKI on CKD; HCO₃ 16 = metabolic acidosis shifting K⁺ out of cells; mild hyponatraemia fits volume depletion
Causes
Four at once: CKD 4 baseline · AKI on top (gastro, poor intake) · ramipril + spironolactone additive · acidosis. Then ask: OTC NSAIDs, recent trimethoprim, potassium salt substitutes
Management

Three jobs: PROTECT calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–3 min on the monitor, repeat at 5 min if ECG unchanged, lasts 30–60 min, does NOT lower K⁺ · SHIFT 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL 50% glucose IV over 15–30 min, hourly BGL for ≥6 h unprompted, plus salbutamol 10–20 mg neb; consider bicarbonate given HCO₃ 16 (weak evidence) · REMOVE oliguric, eGFR 16 → haemodialysis is definitive, renal team + retrieval now. Withhold ramipril and spironolactone, cautious volume, recheck K⁺ at 1–2 h
Patient

Explain the effect, never the number: 'a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be … upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart … calcium protects the heart while the rest works … two of your tablets hold potassium in — stopping both today, don't restart until reviewed'. Answer heart attack / my fault / Adelaide honestly; offer to call someone
ask: ★ Examiner, before I go through these in full — the potassium is 7.2, which is in the severe range. I would attach cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately, and I would check whether the sample was reported as haemolysed.

Examiner's three questions after management, in order: 'Does the calcium lower his potassium?' → No — stabilises the myocardium, serum level unchanged, must always be given alongside something that shifts or removes K⁺, never instead. 'Commonest complication of your treatment?' → hypoglycaemia from insulin, often delayed, hence hourly BGL for 6 h. 'ECG had been normal — would you still treat?' → yes, K⁺ 7.2 is treated on the level; a normal ECG is not permission to wait

To the patient: 'Am I going to have a heart attack?' → 'Not a heart attack in the usual sense — this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery. I don't want to understate it — at this level the rhythm can become dangerous, which is why you're on a monitor and I'm treating you now. It is very treatable.'

'Is it something I did? I couldn't keep anything down.' → 'You have not done anything wrong. Being unwell and dehydrated strained kidneys that were already struggling, and two of your tablets hold potassium in — that combination caused this.'

'Do I have to go to Adelaide?' → 'Possibly. If the potassium doesn't come down with treatment, dialysis is the most effective way to remove it and that means transferring you. I'm arranging that conversation now so we aren't delayed. Is there someone you'd like me to call?'
If he looks blank at '7.2 — is that bad?' you have quoted the number instead of the effect — restart in lay terms

Drugs to stop: ramipril, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim; hold metformin with eGFR 16 and acute illness VERIFY

Version B run (K⁺ 6.1, well 44-year-old woman, pre-procedure bloods): order of operations — ECG and observations FIRST, ask about haemolysis/delayed processing/platelet and white cell counts, THEN repeat with wide-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet or fist clenching, prompt transport — THEN conclude pseudohyperkalaemia; do not treat and do not cancel the procedure until a clean result; if repeat high, it's real → renal function, medications, adrenal causes

fails: Not asking for an ECG and monitoring in the first response — a fail regardless of the total ★
Calcium gluconate without dose and route; or not stating that calcium does NOT lower potassium ★
No hourly glucose monitoring, unprompted ★
Not withholding ramipril and spironolactone ★
Naming one cause and stopping; reading the whole panel before asking for the ECG; quoting '7.2' at the patient; false reassurance on the heart-attack question
Not naming dialysis as definitive here; not involving renal / retrieval early

Severe ≥6.5 or any ECG change; moderate 6.0–6.4 (Version B 6.1) VERIFY · recheck K⁺ 1–2 h

setting: You are an HMO in a metropolitan emergency department.
stem: A 52-year-old man has presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath that started one hour ago. The pain began while he was chopping wood.
Vital signs: BP 135/85 · pulse 78 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on room air · T 36.8°C. He has no history of bleeding disorders.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your management plan to the patient

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI — ST elevation in I, aVL and V2–V6 with reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF; most likely proximal LAD; sinus rhythm ~65–70, normal axis, normal PR, narrow QRS, no established Q waves. Treat as time-critical: primary PCI within 90 min (metro). James Whitfield, self-employed builder, smoker 15/day, untreated BP, father died of MI at 58, no bleeding problems, no sildenafil. Hidden agenda: terrified of dying like his father; money — two jobs booked, no income if he stops. Discriminating behaviour: 'six things, one at a time' — every drug with dose and route, the sildenafil question attached to the nitrate, oxygen refused with the 92% threshold, PCI translated.
plan: Park the patient in one sentence: 'I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly — I've been asked to look at your heart tracing with my examiner first, give me one minute.' If 'am I having a heart attack?' → 'that's exactly what I'm checking and I'll tell you straight away'

ECG in fixed order: details/date/calibration → rate → rhythm → axis → PR → QRS → ST segments (elevation V2–V6, I, aVL; reciprocal III, aVF) → no Q waves → impression anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

Say 'heart attack' plainly with plain-words mechanism; 'I've already let the cardiac team know'; acknowledge the father. Then: (1) aspirin 300 mg chewed + clopidogrel 600 mg (2) GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3 — ask Viagra/Cialis in last 24 h FIRST, say the other contraindications (3) IV access (4) troponin + FBC/UEC/lipids/coags — 'we are not waiting for it'; morphine 2.5–5 mg IV, ondansetron 4–8 mg IV

(5) oxygen only if SpO2 <92%, repeat ECG 1–2 hourly (6) PCI within 90 min: fine tube from wrist/groin, dye, balloon or stent — translate every word; cardiology consent. 'Are you cutting my chest open?' → no, a needle puncture at the wrist

'Am I going to die?' — no false promise: serious, caught early, treatment works well, I'm staying with you. Offer to call Karen. Ask for concerns (money → social work). One-line summary. If time remains: DAPT 12 months then aspirin, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker, cardiac rehab, smoking, driving — never drift into history taking
ask: Hello James — I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. Give me one minute with my examiner and I'll come straight back with the plan.

Examiner, this is a 12-lead ECG; I'd confirm patient details, date and calibration. Rate ~65–70 (R–R about 4½ large squares). Regular, P before every QRS — sinus. Axis normal. PR normal and constant, QRS narrow. ST elevation V2–V6 and I, aVL — ≥1 mm limb, ≥2 mm V2–V3; reciprocal ST depression III and aVF. No established Q waves. Impression: acute anterolateral STEMI, likely proximal LAD, time-critical.

The tracing shows that you are having a heart attack. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart muscle has become blocked by a clot, so part of that muscle isn't getting blood and oxygen — that's the pain. It is serious. It is also very treatable and we're starting right now. I've already let the cardiac team know.
There are six things I'm going to do in the next few minutes. Let me take them one at a time.

★ Before I give you the spray — one question I have to ask everybody: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours? ('why?' → together they can drop your blood pressure dangerously low)
How long for the blood test? → 'It doesn't change what we do today — we're not waiting for it. The tracing is enough to act on; waiting would cost you heart muscle.'
Shouldn't I be on oxygen? → 'It's 97% which is good; extra oxygen doesn't help and can narrow the heart arteries — if it falls below 92% I'll start it.'

Am I going to die? → 'I'm not going to pretend this isn't serious — it is. But you got here fast, we've caught it early, and the treatment works well. I'm going to stay with you.' Is there anyone you'd like me to call? Any questions or concerns?

Investigations: ECG within 10 min of arrival, repeat 1–2 hourly; troponin (named, then discounted as a reason to wait), FBC, UEC, lipids, coags; continuous monitoring

Reperfusion Version A: primary PCI — target 90 min, acceptable if reachable within 120 min of first medical contact; translate 'percutaneous coronary intervention' → fine tube from the wrist, dye, ballooning, stent = tiny metal scaffold; awake but comfortable; cardiology consents

Long-term if time allows: aspirin + clopidogrel 12 months then aspirin 100 mg lifelong, atorvastatin 40–80 mg / rosuvastatin 20–40 mg, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker once stable, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking (Quitline 13 7848), diet, activity, driving restrictions VERIFY

Summary: 'your tracing shows a heart attack; aspirin and clopidogrel to stop the clot growing, a spray and morphine for the pain, and the cardiac team is preparing to reopen the artery within the hour. I'll be right here.'

setting: You are the Hospital Medical Officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan Australian hospital.
stem: James Whitfield, a 55-year-old man, has presented with the sudden onset of central chest pain that began approximately 20 minutes ago. He is anxious and says his father died of a heart attack.
BP 124/78 · pulse 98 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 98% room air · temp 37.8 °C · BGL 5.6 (exact vitals vary between recalls — the pattern is stable with a low-grade fever).
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will be shown an ECG — give the examiner your overall impression and the key features that support it
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Version A — the ECG is handed over after the history (mini-bell / prompt at about 4 minutes in the face-to-face format). Stop the history when the bell goes.

back.dx: Acute pericarditis, most likely viral — the case that looks exactly like an MI until the last SOCRATES question. Central, crushing, sudden, 20 min, constant, 7/10, to left arm and jaw … then BETTER LEANING FORWARD, worse lying flat, sharper on deep breath, flu ten days ago, feverish and tired, no CV risk factors (never smoked, clear check-up). The role-player sits leaning forward clutching his chest — look at him. ECG: rate ~100, sinus, normal PR/QRS, concave ST elevation I, II, V2–V6 (crosses territories), no reciprocal depression except aVR, PR depression. Discriminating behaviour: finish SOCRATES before opening the differential; never say 'definitely not a heart attack' before the troponin.
plan: Vitals from examiner → 'haemodynamically stable'; wash; intro, confirm name; open question; acknowledge the father's death — 'I'll come back to that'; signpost + consent
SOCRATES to the end — the box is sealed until E: 'anything make it worse? better? — I notice you're sitting forward holding your chest, is it easier like that? and lying flat? deep breath or cough?'
Associated + prodrome: cold/flu in last 1–2 weeks, feverish, tired

Kill list in one block: MUST ASK CVS (exertional pain before today, sweating/nausea/doom, tearing to back, arms different, palpitations, blackouts, oedema, orthopnoea/PND) · MUST ASK resp (sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf pain/swelling, travel/surgery/immobility, fever/cough/sweats/weight loss) · GI (burning, meals, acid, forceful vomiting before pain, black stools) · MSK/skin (injury, lifting, tender on pressing, rash/burning skin) · psych (stress, panic, tingling)
SADMA (cocaine/amphetamines; anticoagulants), PMHx (DM/HTN/lipids, previous MI, cardiac surgery, autoimmune, cancer, TB, HIV, renal), FHx with age, ICE 'what are you most worried this might be?'
Bell → excuse yourself → ECG in seven steps → impression in four words: widespread · doesn't match a territory · no reciprocal · concave (+ PR depression)

Diagnosis in plain words + THREE reasons (leans forward, recent flu — most are viral, the tracing) · honest troponin line · long DDx one clause each, killers first · plan: troponin, CXR, echo, FBE/ESR/CRP, admit, colchicine + NSAID, no strenuous exercise · safety-net · summary · questions

That sounds very frightening and I can see you're uncomfortable. I'm going to take a history and then examine you so I can come to a diagnosis and make a plan — is that okay?
Where exactly? When — sudden or gradual? Sharp, dull, crushing, tight? Move anywhere? Constant or comes and goes? Out of ten?

★ Anything make it worse? Anything make it better? — 'I notice you're sitting forward and holding your chest — is the pain easier when you lean forward like that? And what happens if you lie flat?' Does it change with a deep breath or cough?
★ Any cold or flu-like symptoms in the last week or two? Felt feverish or unusually tired?

Exertional chest pain before today? Sweating, nausea, a feeling of doom? Tearing pain through to the back? Pain different in each arm? Palpitations? Blackouts? Leg swelling? Breathless lying flat or waking at night?
Sudden breathlessness? Coughing up blood? Calf pain or swelling? Long flights, car trips, surgery, time in bed? Fever, productive cough, night sweats, weight loss?

Burning pain, worse lying down or after meals? Acid coming up? Forceful vomiting before the pain? Black stools? Injury, heavy lifting? Tender when pressed? Rash or blistering? Stress, panic, tingling?

Smoke? Alcohol? Cocaine or amphetamines? Regular medicines — any blood thinners? Allergies? Diabetes, BP, cholesterol, previous heart problems or surgery, autoimmune disease, cancer, TB, HIV, kidney problems? Family — heart attack or sudden death, and at what age? What are you most worried this might be?

'So it's definitely not a heart attack?' → 'It looks much more like pericarditis — but the two can look very similar and I won't tell you a heart attack is excluded until the troponin blood test is back. That test is the main reason I'd like to keep you in hospital.'

Explain: 'the heart sits inside a thin covering, a bit like a sac; in pericarditis that covering becomes inflamed and that is the pain'. SOB, sweating, nausea, racing heart? Fever/chills/flu? Breathless flat, leg swelling? Fainted with exercise? Calf pain, travel, clots? Injury? Cough, blood? Weight loss? Tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste? Pressing/rash? Stress, mood?

★ Family history of heart attacks or strokes? High sugar, high BP, high fats? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol? Overweight? Medications — including anything like Viagra? Recreational drugs? Allergies? Anything else?
'Are you sure?' → 'I understand this is a shock. I'm confident for three reasons…'
pefe: Poor-image technique: say you're zooming in; compare each ST segment to the isoelectric (TP) line, not to expectation; one small square named in a lead is a real finding; anchor on what you can genuinely see and build to neighbouring and opposite leads; never invent a finding

Model paragraph: 'technically difficult, but rate, rhythm, P waves, PR and QRS are normal. ST elevation of about one small square in I and aVL, and across V2–V6. Because the elevation is widespread I specifically examined the inferior leads for reciprocal change — about 1 mm of ST depression in III and aVF. Reciprocal change argues against pericarditis. Diagnosis: acute anterolateral STEMI'

Case B full explanation under 60 s: heart attack — blood tube blocked → three reasons → dissection (not likely), PE (no travel), pneumothorax (no injury) reasoned → then food-pipe tear, covering of the heart, narrowed valve, heart failure, pneumonia, lung cancer, rib joints, shingles, reflux, ulcer

Anterolateral vs pericarditis vs inferior: elevation I, aVL, V1–V6 convex/straight with reciprocal III, aVF ± II · widespread concave, no reciprocal, aVR depressed · II, III, aVF with reciprocal I, aVL, check V1
Plan: aspirin, pain relief, monitor, cardiology called, cath lab, CCU, tell us if pain worsens or faint; management detail as MED-21
fails: Calling widespread elevation pericarditis without checking the opposite leads ★
Skipping the risk factor block ★
Leading with the impression; freezing on a poor-quality tracing; dismissing one small square because it isn't dramatic
Cardiac-only screen; no list when the bell rings; talking over the bell; no plan or safety-net
numbers: The one question this station tests: 'have I looked at the opposite leads?' — reciprocal present = infarct; absent + concave + aVR depression = pericarditis
Compare to the isoelectric TP segment · 1 small square = 1 mm = a real finding when named in a lead
Three modifiable risk factors here (HTN, DM, lipids) + smoking + weight + FHx at 60 · dad at 60 is not premature (<55) but still counts as family history
Aspirin 300 mg chewed · ECG within 10 min · activate STEMI pathway before troponin · see MED-21 for the full drill and management
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You are a GP at a suburban general practice in Australia.
stem: Mr Daniel Reid, a 40-year-old man, has presented today complaining of chest pain.
Vital signs recorded by the practice nurse: temp 37.8 °C · HR 88 · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% RA · BGL not done. Haemodynamically stable — you may proceed with a focused consultation.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (~4 min)
Review the physical examination findings provided on the screen (Version B face-to-face: ask the examiner for the findings)
Explain your provisional diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your investigations and initial management, including safety-netting
time: 8 minutes. About 4 minutes of history, then findings, explanation, plan and safety-net.

back.dx: Herpes zoster of the right T4 dermatome — sharp stabbing pain from the right nipple round to the back, same side, never crossing the midline, started last night, 8–9/10, constant, worse overnight, ALLODYNIA (the bedsheet brushing the skin), burning/itching for a day or two before, flu last week, feverish and tired. Co-diagnosis the station is built around: why is a 40-year-old reactivating varicella? — 5 kg weight loss, night sweats, exhaustion, a lump under the right arm (firm 2 cm axillary node on exam) → lymphoma/leukaemia screen. Childcare worker; pregnant sister staying at home. Version B trap (2019): examiner says 'no rash' — the pain precedes the rash by 2–3 days; the diagnosis stands. Findings on screen: low-grade fever; vesicular rash on one side of the chest not crossing the midline (= dermatomal — decode it); CVS and resp normal; ECG normal.
plan: Vitals acknowledged → wash → intro, name/DOB → open question → empathy → consent; chest exposure with privacy and chaperone offer
SOCRATES: point to it → 'does it ever cross to the other side?' → sharp/stabbing → allodynia → 'tingling, burning or numb?' → severity, sleep

Exclude the killers even though you 'know': exertional? to jaw/arm, sweating, nausea? SOB, haemoptysis? calf, travel, surgery? ★ 'you had the flu — worse lying flat, better sitting forward?' (pericarditis) · heartburn, meals, swallowing · injury, lifting, coughing

Shingles layer: rash or blisters seen? ★ occupation ★ contacts (pregnant, newborns, young children, immunosuppressed) → ★ malignancy red flags: weight loss, drenching sweats, lumps in neck/armpit/groin, bruising/bleeding, fevers, tiredness → diabetes symptoms → steroids/immunosuppressants → HIV/BBV risk with a preface → chickenpox as a child, previous shingles, vaccine → eye/ear symptoms
SADMA, PMHx (DM, cancer, HIV, autoimmune, transplant, renal), FHx, who's at home, 'what were you most worried this might be?' (heart attack — address it first later)

Findings: decode 'vesicles one side, not crossing midline' = dermatomal, right T4; note the axillary node. Version B: ask by name (general/cachexia, vitals + BGL, lymph nodes + hepatosplenomegaly, CVS incl. rub, resp, chest wall — rash? crosses midline? tenderness incl. light touch, neuro with dermatomal sensory testing, abdomen, ECG, urinalysis)

Heart worry first (exam + ECG normal, pattern doesn't fit) → shingles in plain words → DDx → the second conversation: why now, honest 'is it cancer?' → investigations → four-part management → contacts, work, notification → safety-net incl. PHN → summary, written info, review 2–3 days
ask: Show me exactly where. Does it ever cross over to the other side of your chest? Tight or heavy, or sharp? ★ 'Even the bedsheet hurts' → is the skin also tingling, burning or numb? Out of ten, and has it stopped you doing anything?

Does it come on when you exert yourself? Spread to jaw, neck, left arm? Sweating, nausea, faint? Shortness of breath, coughing blood? Calf swelling or pain, long flights, surgery, time in bed? ★ You had the flu — is it worse lying flat and better sitting forward? Heartburn, related to eating, difficulty swallowing? Injury, heavy lifting, hard coughing?
Noticed any rash or blisters on that area? ★ What do you do for work — children or healthcare? ★ Contact with anyone pregnant, any newborns or young children, anyone with a weak immune system?

★ 'Some questions may seem unrelated' — lost weight without trying? Drenching night sweats? Lumps in neck, armpits or groin? Unusual bruising or bleeding? Persistent fevers? More tired than usual? Drinking or passing urine more? Known diabetes? Steroids, chemotherapy, arthritis or bowel-disease drugs, injections affecting the immune system? 'I ask everyone — anything in your background that might affect your immune system, such as blood-borne virus risk?' Chickenpox as a child? Shingles before? Vaccinated? Rash near the eye, forehead, tip of nose, eye pain, vision change? Ear pain, hearing, dizziness, facial weakness?
Smoke, alcohol, drugs, medications, allergies? Past conditions? Family — heart disease, clots, cancer? Who's at home? What were you most worried this might be?

'Is it cancer?' → 'I can't tell you today and I don't want to alarm you. These symptoms need proper investigation rather than ignoring. Some causes are straightforward — diabetes, a recent infection. Others involve the blood or lymph glands, and those are the ones I want to find or rule out, because finding them early matters.'
pefe: Version B ordered request: 1 general — distress, cyanosis, pallor, drowsy, cachexia 2 full vitals incl. BGL 3 lymph nodes cervical/supraclavicular/axillary/inguinal + hepatosplenomegaly 4 full CVS incl. JVP and pericardial rub, calves 5 resp 6 chest wall — 'is there any rash? does it cross the midline? tenderness on palpation and to light touch?' 7 neuro upper/lower limbs + dermatomal sensory testing over the band 8 abdomen 9 ECG, BGL, urinalysis

'No rash' answer: 'The absence of a rash does not exclude shingles — the pain typically precedes the rash by a few days. My provisional diagnosis remains herpes zoster, and I would warn him a rash is likely over the next 2–3 days and review within 48–72 h so antivirals start inside the window'

Explain: heart worry first → 'shingles — when you had chickenpox the virus went to sleep in the nerve roots near your spine; years later it can wake up and travel along one nerve — that's why the pain is a band on one side that stops dead in the middle, and why the skin is so sensitive. The pain usually comes first and the rash a few days later.' DDx: heart, clot on the lung, sac around the heart, lung infection, reflux, chest-wall cartilage — unlikely on history, exam and ECG

Investigations — two jobs, say both: (1) confirm/exclude mimics: ECG (mandatory), swab from a de-roofed vesicle for VZV PCR (don't wait for it — clinical diagnosis), troponin only if ischaemic suspicion (2) why now: FBE + film, BGL/HbA1c, HIV serology with consent, ESR/CRP, LDH, UEC (antiviral dosing), LFT, CXR (mediastinal nodes) → urgent haematology if abnormal

Management: 1 antiviral — famciclovir 500 mg TDS × 7 days (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS × 7, or aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7); within 72 h of rash if immunocompetent, any duration if immunocompromised; renal dose adjustment VERIFY 2 analgesia — not paracetamol alone: regular paracetamol + NSAID, paracetamol/codeine for breakthrough with constipation advice, early amitriptyline/gabapentin/pregabalin if severe 3 skin — cool compresses, calamine, clean/dry, loose clothing, non-adherent dressing, don't scratch 4 contacts — until every blister has crusted avoid pregnant women who haven't had chickenpox, newborns, unvaccinated young children, immunosuppressed; cover, hand-wash, no shared towels; 'the fluid gives chickenpox, not shingles' · off work while lesions can't be covered, medical certificate, check childcare requirements · notifiable in SA (say you'll comply) VERIFY · review 2–3 days · Shingrix once recovered if eligible (NIP ≥65, ATSI ≥50, immunocompromised ≥18) VERIFY

Safety-net: rash near eye/forehead/nose tip (Hutchinson's) or eye pain/vision → same-day ophthalmology · rash spreads, crosses midline, >20 lesions → disseminated, admit IV aciclovir · facial weakness, hearing, vertigo → Ramsay Hunt, ENT · hot red spreading skin/pus · high fever, confusion, new SOB, worsening chest pain. PHN warning: 'the rash settles but the nerve pain can outlast it — come back, there are specific medicines'
fails: Not exploring an underlying cause for zoster at 40 — no concern over weight loss and tiredness, no malignancy/immunosuppression screen — documented CRITICAL ERROR ★
Ruling out shingles because the examiner says 'no rash' ★
No ECG in a chest pain station; committing to shingles before excluding ACS, PE, pericarditis
Paracetamol alone for severe neuropathic pain; delaying antivirals for the PCR
No contact advice, no occupation question, no notification; exposing the chest without consent/chaperone offer
'It's only a rash'; jargon (herpes zoster, dermatomal, dorsal root ganglion) untranslated; no PHN warning, no review date
numbers: 72 hours — antiviral window from rash onset (immunocompetent); any duration if immunocompromised (diabetes, steroids, malignancy, HIV count)
Famciclovir 500 mg 8-hourly × 7 · valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly × 7 · aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7 · reduce in renal impairment · IV aciclovir if disseminated/immunocompromised VERIFY
Dermatomes: T4 nipple · T6 xiphisternum · T10 umbilicus · C6 thumb · L4 medial malleolus — name 'right T4' to the examiner
Rash: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base → pustules → crusts over 7–10 days; pain precedes rash by 2–3 days (up to a week); infectious until crusted
Red-flag distributions: ophthalmic (Hutchinson's sign, nose tip) · Ramsay Hunt (ear vesicles + facial palsy) · disseminated (>20 lesions outside the dermatome / crossing midline)
Shingrix NIP: ≥65, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ≥50, immunocompromised ≥18 VERIFY · SA Health notification · PATS/Country Health Connect · ACCHS · TIS National 131 450

stem: Your next patient is Margaret Doyle, 65, who was admitted two weeks ago with pneumonia, treated with antibiotics, discharged, and is now well. She has a permanent pacemaker for a bradyarrhythmia and uses CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea. She plans to travel interstate in two weeks. Two chest X-rays are available: the admission film and a repeat film taken this week.
Observations: T 36.6 °C · P 72 regular · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% room air.
tasks: Explain the two chest X-rays to the patient
Take a relevant focused history
Counsel her about the risks of travelling and advise her accordingly
time: 8 minutes. 0:30 films · 1:30 pneumonia box · 2:30 pacemaker/CPAP · 3:45 risk factors/SADMA · 4:30 the trip · 5:15 verdict and counselling · 7:30 summary and safety-net.

back.dx: Fit to travel — resolved right middle lobe pneumonia (admission film: dense white patch right mid-zone, pacemaker box with two leads; this week's film: cleared, sharp heart border), symptoms settled, SpO2 97%. Two things she will NOT volunteer: CPAP only two nights a week (mask digs into her nose) and ten cigarettes a day for forty years. 'Somac' = pantoprazole — say it. Cairns, ten days, three-hour flight, staying with sister Anne — and a beginner scuba dive is booked (surfaces only if you ask what she'll do). Discriminating behaviours: hold the verdict until the history is done; ask 'how many nights a week' not 'do you use it'; ask what she plans to do; letter + written red flags because she'll be 2,500 km away.
plan: WIPE, confirm name; open question; agenda: films → recovery, heart and sleep apnoea, the trip → clear answer + something in writing

Films: three colours → heart, spine, windpipe → normal left lung first → right mid-zone white patch → NAME the pacemaker → second film: black again, sharp heart border → 'cleared completely' → 'I think the answer will be yes — let me check a few things first'
Box 1 pneumonia: admitted/discharged, days of antibiotics and finished?, cough, sputum, BLOOD, SOB walking/lying flat, fever/chills/sweats, chest pain, appetite and WEIGHT
Box 2: pacemaker — when, last check, tablets, racing/fluttering, dizzy spells/blackouts; CPAP — 'how many nights a week do you actually use it?' → two → acknowledge, flag you'll come back
Box 3: asthma/emphysema, diabetes, kidney/liver, cancer, steroids, stroke/memory/choking; medications (Somac = pantoprazole); flu and pneumonia vaccines; smoke — how much; alcohol; occupation
Box 4: where, when, how long; flying or driving; who with, staying with whom; WHAT will you do; insurance, enough medication

Verdict: yes — 'no rule that you must wait a set time after a pneumonia'. Letter (admission, antibiotics, pacemaker, CPAP settings). Red flags + 000 + tell your sister. No scuba (snorkelling fine; formal dive medical if she insists, later). CPAP: consequences, mask refit/nasal pillows/humidifier, sleep service referral, take it on the plane. Smoking: ask-advise-assess-assist-arrange in 90 s, Quitline 13 7848, NRT. Flu vaccine today, check pneumococcal and COVID. Tropical advice, flight advice
Summary in one breath; 'have I missed anything you were worried about?'
ask: 'On an X-ray there are really only three colours: white is bone, grey is soft tissue like heart and muscle, black is air. Here is your heart, your spine, your windpipe down the middle. Your left lung is completely black — normal. Compare the right: a dense white patch here in the middle — that's where the infection was. And this box with two wires into your heart is your pacemaker, correctly placed, wires intact.'

'Second film — same colours, same landmarks, same pacemaker — but the area that was white is black again, and the heart edge is sharp. Your pneumonia has cleared completely. I think the answer will be yes; before I commit, let me ask about your recovery, your heart and sleep apnoea, and the trip.'

When admitted, when home? Days of antibiotics — finished? Still coughing, bringing anything up? ★ Any blood in it? Breathless walking or lying flat? Fever, chills, night sweats since? Chest pain? Appetite and weight?

Pacemaker — when put in, last checked? Any heart tablets, taken daily? Racing, fluttering, funny beating? Dizzy spells or blackouts? ★ 'And the sleep apnoea — how many nights a week do you actually use the CPAP?' → 'Thank you for being honest — I want to come back to that, there are things we can do about the mask'

Asthma or emphysema? Diabetes, kidney, liver, cancer? Steroid tablets? Stroke, memory trouble, choking on food or drink? What medications? ('Somac is pantoprazole — that settles acid') Flu and pneumonia vaccinations up to date? ★ Do you smoke, how much? Alcohol? What did you do for work?
★ Where are you going, when, how long? Flying or driving? Who with, staying with whom? What are you planning to do while you're there? Travel insurance, enough of your medications?
'Yes, you can make this trip. Symptoms settled, oxygen normal, repeat film clear — there is no rule you must wait a set time after a pneumonia; what matters is that you've recovered, and you have.'

'One thing I'd steer you away from: the scuba dive. Diving puts the lungs under pressure and so soon after a pneumonia there's a real risk of lung injury. Snorkelling on the surface is fine. If you genuinely want to dive you need a formal dive medical first — and I'd rather that waited.'
pefe: No examination task. If the examiner asks for a doctor-level read: erect PA films; admission — right middle lobe consolidation with loss of the right heart border, dual-chamber pacemaker in situ with leads in the right atrium and right ventricle, no effusion; repeat — resolution of consolidation, right heart border restored
The letter: admission dates, antibiotic given, pacemaker (model/date), CPAP settings, medications, allergies, GP contact; hand over to any doctor in Cairns

Red flags, written: cough returning or worsening · more breathless · fever or chills · chest pain · coughing up blood · feeling faint → see a doctor; severe → 000; tell Anne so she can act if you can't

CPAP counselling: two nights a week = the discomfort without the benefit; untreated OSA → repeated overnight desaturation, higher BP, strain on a heart that already needs a pacemaker, more chest infections; fixes — different mask size, nasal pillows, humidifier; refer back to the sleep service for a refit; take the machine on the plane (airlines carry it as medical equipment — noted in the letter)

Smoking, 90 seconds: 'I won't lecture you, but at ten a day smoking is the biggest single thing making another pneumonia likely — and the one thing we can change. Have you thought about stopping?' → Quitline 13 7848 (they ring you back), nicotine patch + lozenge/gum, review a fortnight after she's home. Never moralise; if she says 'after the trip', accept it as a start

Vaccines and travel: influenza today (adjuvanted from 65), check pneumococcal (funded at 70; from 50 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander; earlier with risk conditions) and COVID booster; up there — avoid coughs and crowded indoor places while the lungs finish healing, repellent, don't drink from creeks, wet season keep cuts covered and out of mud; on the flight drink water and walk about
SA: Country Health Connect for the sleep-service referral pathway if rural; healthdirect 1800 022 222; TIS 131 450
fails: Answering 'yes, off you go' after the films and losing the history — or never giving a clear verdict at all ★
Accepting 'yes I've got the machine' — never asking how many nights ★
Never asking about smoking, or not quantifying it
Not asking what she'll do on the trip — the dive advice is the only patient-specific advice in the station
Safety-net with nothing written; no letter; no red flags; no 000

Starting the film with the abnormality; not naming the pacemaker; not comparing the two films; turning smoking into a full cessation consult; lecturing (she becomes defensive: 'I've heard all this before')
numbers: Quitline 13 7848 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450 · 000

Radiographic clearance normally 4–6 weeks · repeat film at 6 weeks in smokers over 50 · CURB-65 and SMART-COP ≥3 are severity tools at presentation, NOT travel tools · cabin altitude equivalent 1,500–2,500 m VERIFY
Influenza annually, adjuvanted from 65 · pneumococcal funded at 70 (50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults; earlier with risk conditions) VERIFY current NIP
Long-term PPI is a modest pneumonia risk factor · OSA untreated → hypertension, arrhythmia, higher infection risk · CPAP adherence target ≥4 h/night on ≥70% of nights VERIFY

Variant 1 examiner: 'what is her risk score?' → 'there is no validated risk score for travel after pneumonia; I assessed her under four headings — complete resolution, comorbidity control, ongoing risk factors, demands of the trip — and she is fit, with two modifiable risks addressed'

Variant 2 still symptomatic, shadow not cleared: 'my advice is different from what you hoped' — persistent cough and incomplete clearance at 65 with a smoking history → bloods and CT chest before travel to be certain nothing sits behind the infection; postpone a few weeks; book the scan this week
Variant 3 overseas: destination vaccines, food/water, mosquitoes, insurance with declared pre-existing conditions, medications in hand luggage with a letter, nearest reliable facility

stem: Jenny Alcott, 60, has been brought to your practice. She has been breathless for two months and has been coughing up red / pink sputum.
Observations on request: BP 124/76 · pulse 96 regular · RR 22 · SpO2 91% on room air, 95% on 2 L via nasal prongs · T 36.9 °C. Face-to-face she is on an oxygen mask.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 5 minutes)
A chest X-ray is provided at 5 minutes — explain it to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History 5 min · film ≤1 min · diagnosis, reasoning and differentials 2 min.

back.dx: Small right pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer — two months of progressive exertional breathlessness ('can't get enough air'), now some breathlessness at rest, pink/streaky red sputum five or six times in a fortnight (a few drops, no clots), dry cough, 5 kg weight loss since Easter, poor appetite, very tired; retired aged-care nurse; smoked ten years in her twenties; no asbestos, no fevers/sweats/travel, one pillow, no oedema. Film: blunted right costophrenic angle, sharp left angle, trachea central. DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: 'pleural effusion' is a sign, not a diagnosis — name the finding, then name the cause as 'a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung', justified from her own findings.
plan: Vitals — REACT to SpO2 91%: 'her saturations are low, so I'd keep her oxygen on while we talk'. WIPE, open question, acknowledge the fear, promise a process

Beat one (90 s): describe the breathlessness (air in / tightness / not enough air), duration, constant, worse?, modifiers → 'does rest help — are you ever breathless at rest?' → sputum: how many times, pink or red, streaks/clots, how much → cough, wheeze
Beat two (70 s): CANCER BLOCK FIRST — weight loss quantified, appetite, lumps, previous cancer, occupation now AND before, asbestos, arm numbness/eyelid/face (Pancoast)

Beat three: chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; family atopy; smoke now OR EVER; childhood chest infections; fever, sore throat, night sweats, travel, TB contact; pillows, leg swelling; rash, joints; tiredness; SADMA only if spare
Film in ≤1 min: three colours → heart, spine, airway central → normal LEFT side first, sharp angle → right angle missing, filled in → 'fluid around the lung — a pleural effusion'

'Breathlessness can have a number of causes — but in your case I have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung' → three reasons (weight loss, blood in sputum, fluid on the film) → pause, acknowledge, support person → differential list → plan (bloods, CT, US-guided pleural tap, urgent respiratory referral) → safety-net → teach-back
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature? → acknowledge the low saturation
'I'm so sorry to hear that, and I understand how worrying it must be. Let me ask a few questions, then I'll go through your chest X-ray with you, find the cause and make the best plan.'

Is it difficulty getting the breath in, tightness, or not enough air? How long? Constant or on and off? Worse? Better or worse with anything? ★ 'You've said it's worse walking — does rest make it better? Are you ever breathless at rest, sitting still?'
The pink phlegm — how many times? Pink or frankly red? Streaks or clots? A few drops, a teaspoon, or more? Cough with it? Noisy breathing or wheeze?

★ Cancer block: lost weight without trying — how much, over what period? Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Ever had cancer before? Occupation now — and before that? Asbestos? Numbness or weakness in the arm, anyone comment on your eyelid or face?
Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ 'Do you smoke now, or have you ever smoked?' Recurrent chest infections as a child?
Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose? Night sweats, overseas travel, TB contact? Breathless lying flat — how many pillows? Leg swelling? Rashes, joint pains? Unusually tired?

Film: 'This is an X-ray of your chest. Three colours — white is bone, grey soft tissue, black is air. This big shadow is your heart, down the centre your spine, this line your main airway, sitting nicely central. Start with the normal side: on your left the lung is dark and there's a sharp angle at the bottom where lung meets chest wall. On your right that sharp angle is missing — filled in. That happens when fluid collects around the lung — we call it a pleural effusion.'
pefe: No examination task. If examiner wants a doctor-level read: erect PA, adequate inspiration and penetration, no rotation; blunting of the right costophrenic angle with a meniscus; trachea and mediastinum central; no pneumothorax; no focal bony lesion — small right pleural effusion. Never say this to the patient
Speak in HER sides — the patient's right is on the image left; the marker R sits over her right

Diagnosis: 'I do have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung. I want to explain why, because it isn't a guess: you've been losing weight without trying, you've been coughing up what I believe is blood, and your X-ray shows fluid around the lung. I can't tell you today that that's what it is — but I'm not going to wait either.' → 'I can see that's a shock, I'm sorry to be telling you this today. Take a moment. Is there someone you'd like with you? I'll write everything down.'

Differentials, spoken: infection in the chest including TB (no fevers, sweats, travel) · heart not pumping well (one pillow, no ankle swelling) · liver or kidney problems, underactive thyroid · asthma · smoking damage · scarring from dusts at work · repeated chest infections · low in blood

Plan: FBE, UEC, LFT, TFT; CT chest; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by a specialist (protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S, pH) — 'tells us what the fluid is and often what's causing it; draining some will help your breathing'; urgent respiratory referral; review in a few days regardless; safety-net — much more breathless, more blood, chest pain, fever → straight to hospital

Version B (James Whitlock, 70): massive LEFT effusion with mediastinal shift to the right — 'a large white shadow covering most of the lung, pressing it upward, and your heart has been pushed across'; answer = primary lung cancer OR metastatic prostate cancer (name both, say you can't separate them from the film), third differential occupational lung disease incl. mesothelioma (boilermaker, asbestos) → see MED-26
SA: urgent respiratory referral RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; Aboriginal Liaison Officer if relevant; TIS 131 450
fails: Never saying 'pleural effusion' on the film; or stopping at 'fluid in your lung' without naming the CAUSE ★
Cancer block left to the end 'if there's time'; weight loss not quantified; haemoptysis not characterised; 'do you smoke?' without 'ever' ★
'You have lung cancer' as a verdict — or 'probably nothing serious' as false reassurance; ploughing from the word cancer straight into the list without a pause
Omitting the rest-breathlessness question; forgetting pillows (HF) or travel (TB)
Jargon on the film (costophrenic, opacification); reversing her sides; film over a minute; not reacting to SpO2 91%
Skipping the differential list after naming cancer; no plan, no safety-net
numbers: Film script ≤1 min: three colours → three landmarks → normal side → abnormal side → NAME IT · white = bone, grey = soft tissue, black = air · heart, spine, trachea
Fluid visible ~200 mL on PA, ~50 mL lateral · white-out: shift AWAY = effusion, TOWARDS = collapse, none = consolidation VERIFY

Exudate: cancer, infection/empyema, TB, infarct, connective tissue · transudate: heart failure, liver failure, nephrotic, hypothyroidism · Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, fluid LDH >⅔ ULN VERIFY
Signs: reduced expansion, stony dull, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting · cytology ×3 VERIFY

Four beats: complaint 90 s · cancer block 70 s · sweep 2 min · film + diagnosis + list + plan 3 min · self-check when the film appears: weight quantified, haemoptysis, previous cancer, occupation before, smoking ever

Variant B 'just tell me straight — is it cancer?' → 'I don't know yet — I need the scan and a sample of the fluid. But I won't pretend: cancer is the thing I'm most concerned about, which is why I'm arranging things urgently. You'll hear it from me as soon as I know' · Variant C 78 F, four pillows, oedema, bilateral small effusions, big heart → heart failure, not the cancer recall
Four questions for any named past condition: when · treatment · follow-up · complications
